title: Marriage: The Long Covenant
subtitle: Most marriages do not end in a blowup. They end in a slow drift no one decided on. What Scripture, church history, and honest research say about covenant, conflict, desire, and the daily work of staying married well.

parts.title: The Drift No One Chose
parts.body:
You did not have a fight. That is almost the problem. There was no blowup, no betrayal, no single night you could point to and say there, that is where it cracked. There was only a slow drift, a thousand small turnings away, until one evening you looked across the kitchen at the person you married and realized you had become careful around them. Polite. Two people running a household and a calendar, splitting the logistics of children and money, sleeping in the same bed and living in different countries.

Maybe it is louder than that. Maybe the same argument has been running for nine years under different names, and you can feel the eye roll before it happens, and you have both learned exactly where to cut. Maybe there is a coldness that has hardened into contempt, the quiet conviction that your spouse is the obstacle to the life you were supposed to have. Or maybe it just aches, a low and constant disappointment you do not say out loud because saying it feels like betrayal.

And underneath whatever it is, there is a particular shame for the believer. You stood in front of God and a room full of people and made a promise with the word always in it. So the distance feels like a verdict, not just on the marriage but on your faith. You wonder if a good Christian would feel this. You perform the marriage on Sunday and grieve it on Tuesday, and you tell no one, because telling someone would make it real.

So let me say the thing the wedding industry will not. A hard marriage is not a failed marriage, and the drift is not a sign that you married the wrong person. It is a sign that you married a person. Every marriage between two sinners tends toward entropy the way every garden tends toward weeds, and the couples who make it are not the ones who drifted less. They are the ones who learned to row back.

parts.title: What a Marriage Carries
parts.body:
A marriage is never only about the two people in it, which is exactly why its drift costs so much. A household is the first world a child ever knows, and children learn what love is, what conflict means, and whether the world is safe by watching two adults handle each other in a kitchen. They absorb the temperature of a home long before they understand a word of it. The drift you think is private is being studied every day by small witnesses who will carry it into their own marriages, for good or for ruin. We pass down far more than we teach.

The stakes reach the self as well. You become like the person you sleep beside, slowly, in ways you do not choose. A marriage marked by contempt trains both people in contempt until it leaks into every other relationship they have. A marriage marked by kindness under pressure forms two people who grow gentler with the years. Marriage is not a static arrangement you enter. It is a workshop that is shaping you whether or not you are paying attention, and the only question is what it is shaping you into.

And for the believer there is a weight heavier still. Scripture says marriage is a sign, a living picture of the covenant between Christ and his church, which means a Christian marriage preaches whether or not the couple intends a sermon. When two believers keep faith with each other through the hard years, forgiving as they have been forgiven, the watching world sees something it cannot manufacture and cannot quite explain. And when a Christian marriage curdles into the same cold war as every other, the world concludes that grace changes nothing. The skeptic is not reading your statement of faith. He is reading your anniversary.

parts.title: What Scripture Actually Says About Marriage
parts.body:
Start with the word the culture has lost, covenant. The world offers marriage as a contract, an arrangement between two parties that holds as long as both keep getting what they came for, and dissolves when the value drops. Scripture offers a covenant, a binding promise that creates a new reality and does not depend on the weather. The difference is everything. A contract is protected by an exit. A covenant is protected by a vow. When God describes his own relationship with his people, he never reaches for the language of contract. He reaches for the language of marriage, a love that keeps faith with an unfaithful partner, and that is the love your vows were always pointing at.

Go back to the beginning, to the sentence the whole Bible builds on. A man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh. One flesh is not a metaphor for romance. It is a description of a real union, two lives so joined that to tear them apart is to tear something that has grown together. This is why Scripture treats divorce not as the breaking of a contract but as an amputation, and why even a hard marriage is worth fighting for, because what God has joined has actually been joined.

Then come to the passage couples fear, Ephesians 5, and read it slower than you have been taught to. Paul tells husbands and wives to submit to one another out of reverence for Christ, and then he says something that would have stunned the ancient world. He spends a few words on the wife and a flood of words on the husband, and what he commands the husband is not rule but death. Love your wife as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her. In a culture where the husband held all the power, Paul aims the cross straight at the one holding it. Whatever headship means here, it is defined by a man laying his life down, not throwing his weight around, and any reading that arms a husband instead of crucifying him has read the passage backward.

Scripture is also unembarrassed about desire, which the church too often is. The Song of Songs is in the canon, an unblushing celebration of married longing and delight, God's own answer to the lie that holiness is the enemy of passion. And Paul tells married couples not to deprive one another, treating physical union as a mutual gift and a mutual duty, a guarding of the marriage against the cold. The Bible is more earthy about sex than your youth group ever was, and more serious about it, because it knows that the body is part of the covenant and not a distraction from it.

And running under all of it is the one tool without which no marriage survives, forgiveness. Two sinners cannot share a life without wounding each other, daily, in ways large and small, and a marriage is finally only as durable as its capacity to forgive. Be kind to one another, Paul writes, tenderhearted, forgiving one another as God in Christ forgave you. That is not a decoration on marriage. It is the engine. The couples who last are not the ones who stopped sinning against each other. They are the ones who never stopped forgiving.

parts.title: How the Church Has Understood Marriage
parts.body:
The church has been thinking hard about marriage for two thousand years, and the conversation has not always been wise, which is worth admitting. For long stretches the tradition treated marriage as a concession to weakness, a lower path for those who could not manage celibacy, and elevated the single life as the holier estate. Something real was being protected in that, the goodness of devotion to God above family, but something was also distorted, and ordinary married love was undersold for centuries.

The Reformation recovered the goodness of marriage with force. Luther, a former monk, married a former nun and wrote about the holiness of changing diapers and keeping house, insisting that the kitchen and the marriage bed were arenas of vocation as sacred as the cloister. He called marriage a school for character, a place God uses the friction of shared life to sand down the selfishness no monastery could reach. The Reformers took marriage down from the pedestal of sacrament and planted it back in the soil of daily discipleship, where it could do its actual work.

The Puritans, so often slandered as cold, wrote some of the warmest theology of marriage in the Christian tradition. They insisted that a husband and wife should be, first and most, the best of friends, and that married love should be a delight and not merely a duty. Richard Baxter counseled couples to keep up the affection of the early days on purpose, by attention and kindness, knowing that love left untended cools. They understood what we keep forgetting, that romance is not a feeling that happens to you but a fire that has to be fed.

Across the centuries the church also held a hard line that protected the vulnerable, the permanence of the covenant. In a world where a discarded wife had no standing and no safety, the church's insistence that marriage was for life was not cruelty but shelter. The tradition was not naive about misery. It made room, with care, for the protection of the abused and the abandoned. But it refused to let marriage become a thing you keep only while it pleases you, because it had read its God, who keeps covenant with a people who break it, and concluded that faithfulness through the hard season is the very thing marriage exists to display.

parts.title: Knowledge Tested Against Scripture
parts.body: A believer can study the science of relationships the way a farmer studies the weather, gratefully and critically at once, because all truth is God's truth and the researchers have watched thousands of marriages more closely than most pastors ever will. What follows takes four bodies of secular insight seriously, names what each sees clearly, and tests each against Scripture, because every account of marriage carries a hidden picture of what a person is for.

secular.source: The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work
secular.author: John Gottman
secular.whatItGetsRight: Gottman watched real couples in a laboratory for decades and can predict divorce with unsettling accuracy from how a pair handles conflict. He named the four behaviors that corrode a marriage, criticism, contempt, defensiveness, and stonewalling, and showed that the healthiest couples are not those who avoid conflict but those who repair quickly and keep a high ratio of warmth to friction. This is hard data confirming what Proverbs always said about the soft answer and the corrosive tongue.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Gottman maps the symptoms with great precision and cannot reach the heart that produces them. He can teach you to replace contempt with a gentler start, and he cannot tell you why contempt is there, which Scripture can. Contempt is pride looking down from a height it has no right to, and the cure is not only a communication skill but a person humbled at the foot of the cross, who has seen his own debt forgiven and so loses the standing to despise. The techniques are a real gift. They treat the behavior. The gospel treats the heart the behavior comes from.

secular.author: Amir Levine and Rachel Heller
secular.whatItGetsRight: Attachment research shows that early experiences of care or its absence shape how a person bonds in adulthood, that some reach for closeness anxiously and others flee it, and that much marital conflict is two nervous systems misreading each other through old wiring. Naming the pattern can defuse a fight that was never really about the dishes. It helps a couple see the wound under the weapon.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Scripture agrees that we are shaped by our histories, that the sins and wounds of one generation reach into the next, and it refuses the despair that the past is destiny. Attachment theory can explain why you flinch. It cannot give you a love that casts out fear, and it has no category for the deeper security the gospel offers, a believer anchored not in a spouse's perfect responsiveness but in a Father who will never leave. A marriage asked to heal every old wound will buckle under a weight only God can carry. The theory describes the ache accurately and points it at the wrong healer.

secular.author: Esther Perel
secular.whatItGetsRight: Perel writes honestly about a real tension the church often ignores, that the very closeness and security of a long marriage can dampen desire, which feeds on a measure of distance and mystery. She presses couples to keep tending eros and not assume that comfort and passion automatically coexist. She is naming a true problem that many faithful marriages quietly suffer and few will discuss.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Perel sees the problem clearly and prescribes from a frame Scripture cannot bless, where desire is sovereign and even faithfulness becomes negotiable in its service. The Song of Songs answers her better than she answers herself. It locates the highest erotic delight inside covenant, not against it, an exclusive belonging that intensifies rather than dulls desire because it is utterly safe and utterly committed. The biblical vision does not choose between security and passion. It roots passion in the security, and it refuses to let longing become a license to wander. Tend the fire, Scripture agrees, but tend it at home.

secular.author: Eli Finkel
secular.whatItGetsRight: Finkel shows that modern people ask marriage to do what whole villages and faiths once did, to be soulmate, therapist, best friend, financial partner, and source of self-actualization all at once, and that this expectation crushes the institution under a weight it cannot bear. His sociology is sharp. We have made the spouse into a savior and then resented them for not saving us.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Finkel diagnoses the idolatry exactly and cannot name it as such or cure it. Scripture has a word for asking a finite person to be your everything. It is worship aimed at a creature, and it always ends in disappointment, because no human being was built to bear the weight of a god. The biblical answer is not to expect less of marriage but to stop expecting marriage to be God. A couple who worship together can love each other freely, precisely because they are not demanding salvation from one another. The science sees the overload. Only the gospel takes the burden off.

parts.title: Where Faithful Christians Differ
parts.body: Christians who hold the same Bible and the same high view of marriage still order the roles of husband and wife along two different lines, and the disagreement is serious because both sides are reading the same texts with care. The dividing question is what Scripture means when it speaks of headship and submission in Ephesians 5 and beyond. Hear each view at its strongest, because caricature has done enough damage here.

views.body: This view holds that God created men and women equal in worth and dignity and assigned them distinct and complementary roles, and that marriage is meant to display this design. The husband is called to a headship defined entirely by sacrifice, to lead by laying his life down as Christ did for the church, taking first responsibility for the spiritual health and protection of the home. The wife is called to a glad and intelligent submission to that sacrificial leadership, not a submission of inferiority but of order, the way the Son submits to the Father while remaining fully God. Advocates insist this is the opposite of the domination the world imagines and the church has too often practiced. A husband who uses headship to get his way has forfeited the very thing he claims, because biblical headship is measured by how much he spends himself, not how much he is served. They argue that this pattern, far from oppressing women, protects them, binding a man to a costly responsibility for his wife's flourishing, and that a home ordered this way reflects something true about God that an undifferentiated partnership cannot picture. The danger they name in the other view is a slow erasure of the distinctions Scripture seems to teach, and they hold the line out of fidelity to the text, not love of power.

views.view: Egalitarian: mutual submission and shared authority
views.body: This view holds that in Christ the old hierarchies are undone, that there is neither male nor female in standing before God, and that marriage is meant to display a mutual submission in which both partners lay down their lives for each other. It reads the head of Ephesians 5 in light of the verse that governs the whole passage, submit to one another out of reverence for Christ, and notes that Paul aims his heaviest commands at the husband precisely to dismantle the male dominance of his age rather than to baptize it. Advocates point out that the same Paul commends women leading and teaching, that headship in his letters often carries the sense of source rather than ruler, and that the trajectory of Scripture runs toward the full partnership of equals serving each other. They argue that decisions in a Christian home should be made by two people seeking the mind of Christ together, with authority shared rather than assigned by sex, and that this is not capitulation to the culture but the gospel working out its own logic. The danger they name in the other view is that a structure of male authority, however carefully qualified, has too often given cover to real domination, and they hold their position out of fidelity to the whole counsel of Scripture, not accommodation to the age.

parts.title: What Marriage Forms in You
parts.body:
Marriage is not finally a delivery system for your happiness, though it can hold real happiness. It is, among the things God uses, one of the most relentless instruments of sanctification he has, and the couples who understand this stop asking only whether their marriage is making them happy and start noticing what it is making them into. God did not give you this particular person by accident, and he means to use them to finish you.

He forms the death of the self, which no other relationship presses quite so hard. You can leave a friend who irritates you and change a church that disappoints you, but a spouse is the one mirror you cannot walk away from, the person who knows exactly where your selfishness lives because they have been bruised by it. Marriage will show you that you are far more self-centered than you believed, and that revelation is not the marriage failing. It is the marriage working, exposing the sin that has to die if you are ever to love anyone well.

He forms a covenant love that does not depend on feeling, which is the only kind that lasts. Anyone can love the lovely. Staying tender to a person through the years when they are not lovely, choosing their good when the feeling has gone cold and waiting for the feeling to return, is a love the world cannot generate and only the cross can teach. A husband and wife who keep faith through the dry seasons learn in their own bones how God has loved them, and the learning changes them.

And he forms a long obedience that becomes, slowly, a joy. The couples in their fifth decade who still reach for each other did not arrive there on a feeling. They got there one ordinary act of faithfulness at a time, ten thousand small kindnesses and forgivenesses laid end to end until the path itself became a kind of home. That is what marriage forms in the ones who stay, a love seasoned like old wood, and it is a foretaste of the wedding the whole Bible has been moving toward from the first chapter, the day the covenant God keeps marries the people he will never leave.

parts.title: Practice
parts.body: A marriage is not saved by admiring the theology of marriage. It is saved, or lost, in the small daily acts that either feed the fire or let it go cold. None of what follows is dramatic. All of it works, slowly, if you do it. One note before the list. If there is abuse in your marriage, physical, sexual, or the systematic control and fear that is its quieter form, this section is not your first step. Get to safety and get help now. Call a trusted pastor, a counselor, or in the US the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 800 799 7233. Protecting the vulnerable is not the failure of covenant. It is the keeping of it.

steps: Turn toward, not away, in one small moment a day. When your spouse makes a bid for your attention, the comment about the weather, the story from work, stop what you are doing and meet it. Gottman calls these the small moments that build a marriage. Scripture calls it kindness.

Confess and forgive one specific thing. Not a vague apology for being difficult. Name the actual word or silence that wounded, ask forgiveness for it, and grant it when asked. The marriage runs on this and dies without it.
Pray together once, out loud, even if it is awkward and short. A couple that prays together is doing something no technique can replace, bowing together before the One who holds them both.

Reach for your spouse physically without it being a transaction. A hand held, a long hug at the door. Guard the marriage against the cold the way Scripture says, by tending the body and not only the schedule.

Set a weekly time you protect like a bill that must be paid, an evening or a walk where the phones are down and the children are elsewhere and you are simply two people again. The marriage that gets only the leftovers of your week slowly starves.

Name the one argument that keeps running under different names, and get underneath it together. What is the real thing each of you is afraid of or longing for beneath the dishes and the money. Most perpetual fights are a wound wearing a costume.

Do one concrete thing to tend desire on purpose, because Scripture is unembarrassed about it and so should you be. Pursue your spouse the way you did when you were trying to win them, with attention, with delight, at home.

Find one older couple whose marriage you respect and ask them to coffee with real questions. Marriage wisdom in Scripture travels person to person, and the couples who last are almost always the ones who let someone older in.

If the drift has hardened past what the two of you can reach, get a wise Christian counselor, together, before you are in crisis and not after. Seeing a counselor is not the failure of faith. It is faith walking toward help, the same way you would see a doctor for a body that hurt.

Build a rhythm of forgiveness into the week so the debts do not accumulate. A standing conversation, gentle and honest, where each of you can say what landed wrong and clear it before it calcifies into contempt.

Choose to stay tender through a cold stretch on purpose, loving by covenant when the feeling is gone, and watch for the feeling to return, because in a real marriage it does. This is the love the world cannot make and only the cross can teach.

Put your marriage to work for someone else. The couple who opens their home, mentors a younger pair, and lets their imperfect faithfulness be seen is doing the very thing marriage is for, displaying to a watching world a covenant love that keeps faith through the years, the way God keeps faith with us.
